disease.mechanism: Loss-of-function. Deficiency of Î±-galactosidase A (GLA) impairs lysosomal degradation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), which accumulates in vascular endothelium, kidneys, heart, and nervous system. This causes progressive renal failure, cardiomyopathy, neuropathic pain, and cerebrovascular events.
disease.autotac_rationale: NOT eligible. Fabry disease is a loss-of-function enzyme deficiency — GLA is deficient, not accumulated. Degrading residual enzyme would worsen the disease. Correct route is enzyme replacement therapy (restore GLA) or chaperone therapy, not protein degradation.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 40,000-60,000 males (classic form); higher in some populations — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: Childhood (neuropathic pain, angiokeratomas); renal/cardiac complications in adulthood

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: Recombinant Î±-galactosidase A that replaces the deficient enzyme, restoring Gb3 degradation. Administered intravenously every 2 weeks. Disease-modifying for the non-classic and classic forms.
approved_treatments.note: NOTE: agalsidase beta is a recombinant glycoprotein enzyme (~100 kDa homodimer), NOT a small molecule — MW/PubChem CID left 0 to avoid fabrication.

investigational: Pharmacological chaperone therapy: migalastat (Galafold) — oral, for amenable GLA mutations

disease.human_summary: Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by Î±-galactosidase A deficiency, leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation in the kidneys, heart, and vasculature. It causes progressive renal failure, cardiomyopathy, and neuropathic pain. Enzyme replacement and chaperone therapy are the standard disease-modifying approaches.
